newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia hit by miners strike, defence sacking row.
newsitem.headline: Russia hit by miners strike, defence sacking row.

text.p: Russia faced trouble on two fronts on Tuesday as 400,000 angry coalminers launched a nationwide strike saying they had not been paid for months and a political scandal grew over the sacking of a top general.
Trade union officials said 154 out of Russia's 189 coal pits had stopped work because the government owes the miners at least 1.5 trillion roubles ($300 million) in wages.
Miners' leaders called on Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin to quit, saying his government was to blame.
Chernomyrdin was likely to fly to Siberia to face the miners on his return from the European security summit in Lisbon, Portugal, which ended on Tuesday, Interfax news agency said.
It quoted Gennady Seleznyov, chairman of the lower house of parliament, as saying after meeting President Boris Yeltsin that Chernomyrdin may fly to the Kuzbass mining region.
Some miners planned an indefinite stoppage, while others were halting deliveries to consumers for 24 or 48 hours.

"The strike is huge, probably the biggest, involving about 80 percent of all Russian miners -- we had only one similar strike in February," said Vitaly Budko, head of Coal Miners' Trade Union, who added the miners want the cabinet to resign.
As the Kremlin struggled to cope with the miners' protest, a political scandal gripped the defence ministry.

Defence Minister Igor Rodionov, embroiled in controversy over the sacking of a general, called off a visit to the United States planned for December 4-8 in a clear sign of mounting crisis. The ministry gave no reason for the postponement.
The followed confusion and conflicting statements from the Kremlin and the ministry over the ousting of General Vladimir Semyonov, commander of Russia's ground forces.
The ministry told the press that Semyonov had been sacked "for actions which discredit the honour and dignity of a serviceman and are incompatible with his post".
But Yeltsin's spokesman Sergei Yastrzhembsky said on Tuesday that the ministry had jumped the gun.

Yastrzhembsky told a news briefing that Yeltsin had agreed to Rodionov's request to suspend Semyonov but would not sign his dismissal decree until the case had been considered by a presidential committee on military appointments.
The committee is expected to meet on Wednesday.
Yastrzhembsky said all questions about what he called "this strong formulation" should be addressed to the Defence Ministry. "Somebody was trying to anticipate events," he added.
Semyonov has described charges against him as another attempt to mislead the president and said he had written to Yeltsin to defend himself.
The U.S. embassy in Moscow said it had not yet been informed of the decision, but a defence ministry spokesman told Reuters that a report by Interfax was correct.
